method: Audits the ledger as a document, which validate-claims.py does not: every number in a claim's English text must appear in the artifact it cites, every artifact must exist and parse, every check path must resolve, ids must be unique and contiguous, every claim must carry a limitation, and a claim embargoed from public copy must not be in the README.

text_number_exemptions.912: a line number in the pinned pdjson.c
text_number_exemptions.0: zero is checked by the machine-readable check, not by text matching
text_number_exemptions.1: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.2: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.3: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.4: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.5: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.6: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.7: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.8: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.9: too common to be a useful signal
text_number_exemptions.32: '32- and 64-bit' is prose, not a measurement
text_number_exemptions.30: '30-minute' is prose; the artifact records 1800 seconds
text_number_exemptions.11.8: '11.8 million' is prose; the artifact records the exact case count

limitation: Number matching is textual: a claim saying '6,104 comparisons' passes if 6104 appears anywhere in the artifact, not necessarily as the comparison count. It catches staleness, which is the failure that actually happens; it does not catch a number cited under the wrong label.
